John Lewis. From 1940 to 2020, a towering figure of the civil rights movement who transitioned from Freedom Rider and march organizer to a Georgia congressman serving thirty-four years. His quiet dignity, moral consistency, and legislative longevity made him a living bridge between the movement and post-civil-rights America. He was a founder and leader of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, organizing sit-ins and voting-rights campaigns in the Deep South in the early nineteen-sixties. In 1961 he participated in the Freedom Rides, buses that integrated interstate travel, and was arrested and beaten multiple times by segregationists. Seven years later, he marched across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, suffering a skull fracture from state troopers in what became known as Bloody Sunday. That near-death experience at Selma became an icon of movement sacrifice and commitment. In 1986 he was elected to the House of Representatives from Georgia, and he held that seat for thirty-four consecutive terms until his death in 2020. He authored Walking with the Wind in 1998, a defining memoir of the movement. In Congress, he became known for his quiet moral authority, rarely raising his voice but commanding respect. He rose through SNCC's ranks, serving as national chairman from 1963 to 1966. In his final years, he emerged as a moral voice on democracy, voting rights, and conscience, especially during the Trump presidency.
